slides.page_title: json vs jsonb: What Postgres Stores

items: Both accept RFC 8259 text, same literal syntax
Storage differs completely — that is the whole story
`json` = a text column with a validator
`jsonb` = a data structure
Whitespace stripped on input
Duplicate keys collapsed — last one wins
Object keys reordered: length first, then bytewise
Not insertion order, not alphabetical
Numbers stored as `numeric` — exact, no float artifacts
`NaN` and `Infinity` rejected: no numeric-in-JSON syntax
`jsonb` rejects `\u0000` and any `\uXXXX` the server encoding cannot represent
`json` accepts them on input — checked only for syntactic correctness
`json` errors later: on a processing function or a cast to text
jsonb has equality and a total order
`=`, `<`, `DISTINCT`, `GROUP BY`, whole-value btree all work
`json` has none — `SELECT DISTINCT json_col` is an error

blocks.title: Choose json only when
items: Webhook signature verification
Audit log of raw bodies
Key-order-sensitive clients
You need the byte-exact payload back

blocks.title: Rule Of Thumb
blocks.text: Anything you intend to query, index, or mutate is `jsonb` — which is nearly everything. The 255 MB cap comes from internal offsets; `json`, being text, runs to 1 GB.

items: `to_jsonb(anyelement)` converts any SQL value
`to_jsonb(ROW(1,'x'))`, `to_jsonb(ARRAY[1,2,3])` both work
`row_to_json(t)` / `to_jsonb(t)`: whole row, columns become keys
`jsonb_build_object` is variadic and keeps SQL types
`jsonb_build_array` builds heterogeneous arrays

blocks.title: Never Concatenate
blocks.text: String-building JSON is a JSON-injection bug waiting to happen. `jsonb_build_object` quotes and escapes for you.

items: `jsonb_typeof` is the only reliable way to branch on shape
Six answers: object, array, string, number, boolean, null
Guard length with `WHERE jsonb_typeof(v) = 'array'`
`jsonb_object_keys` is set-returning, objects only
Never store the pretty form — jsonb normalizes it away
`v::text` renders canonical JSON text
`v #>> '{}'` gives a scalar's text with no surrounding quotes
`jsonb_object(ARRAY['a','1','b','2'])` builds from a flat array
The two-array form `jsonb_object(keys, values)` reads cleaner

lines: ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT data_is_obj
-- stops scalars and arrays sneaking into
-- a column meant to hold records

blocks.title: jsonb_strip_nulls(v)
items: Drops object fields whose value is JSON null
Shrinks sparse documents at write time
Leaves nulls inside arrays alone
`->` keeps jsonb so you can keep chaining
`->>` strips the quotes and the type with them
Integer argument indexes arrays; negatives count from the end
Chain rule: `->` for every step except the last

lines: -- one hop, text[] path, digits index

items: `#>` returns jsonb, `#>>` returns text
Both take a `text[]` path and do the whole walk in one hop
Array indexes are written as plain digits inside the path
Missing key returns SQL NULL, never an error — typos fail quietly
`data ->> 'nmae'` is just NULL
Wrong shape is quiet too: integer subscript on an object yields NULL
Text key on an array likewise: NULL, not an error

blocks.title: Tell Them Apart
blocks.text: `data ->> 'k'` is NULL both when the key is absent and when its value is JSON null. Use `data ? 'k'` for existence, or `jsonb_typeof(data->'k')`.

items: `->>` output is `text`, so comparisons are string comparisons
Casting is a runtime landmine, not a compile-time one

lines: -- missing keys created, arrays padded null

items: Subscripts equal `->`: return jsonb, integers index arrays
Assigned value must be jsonb — scalars need quotes and a cast
None of these operators are GIN-indexable on their own
`data->>'x' = 'y'` needs an expression index or a rewrite to `@>`
`@>` asks: is the right side contained in the left side?
The workhorse operator — and the one GIN indexes best
`<@` is `@>` with the operands swapped
Object containment is subset-of-pairs
Array containment ignores order and duplicates
Everything contains the empty structure: `@> '{}'`, `@> '[]'`
A fine no-op filter, a useless index probe

blocks.title: The Scalar Exception
blocks.text: A bare scalar counts as contained in an array — but only at the top level. At depth you must write `@> '{"t":[3]}'`.

items: `?` only ever matches strings: keys, array string elements, top scalar
It never looks at values: `'{"a":"x"}' ? 'x'` is false
Not a substring search
Top level only — no recursive descent
Tag filter: `data @> '{"tags":["sql"]}'` — order-agnostic, index-friendly
It survives the array growing
Multi-key equality is one probe, not three `->>` comparisons
`data @> '{"status":"open","team":"core"}'`

blocks.title: Types Must Match
blocks.text: `@>` matches values by exact JSON type. `@> '{"qty":5}'` will never match a document storing `"qty": "5"`.

items: jsonb values are immutable
Every mutation function returns a new document
There is no in-place patch

slides.page_title: jsonb_set and the Cost of Updates

items: `||` on objects is a shallow merge, right side wins
`||` on two arrays concatenates; non-array plus anything builds an array
`- 'key'` drops a top-level key, `- 2` drops by index
Negative index counts from the end; `- array[...]` drops several
`#- '{a,b}'` deletes at a path, object key or array index alike

blocks.title: No Deep Merge
blocks.text: Postgres ships none. Write a recursive SQL/PLpgSQL function, or merge the leaf paths explicitly.

lines: -- plain 'Cork' is a syntax error: need jsonb

items: With `create_missing = false` a missing path leaves the document untouched
`jsonb_insert(target, path, val [, insert_after])` never overwrites
It errors if the target exists; inserts into arrays at a position

blocks.title: One NULL Wipes The Column
blocks.text: Any SQL NULL argument makes `jsonb_set` return NULL, so the UPDATE blanks the whole document. Guard with `coalesce(...)`.
==TOAST==: any value too wide for the page is stored out of line and compressed; a jsonb update rewrites that whole out-of-line value {green:(full story in the TOAST section)}.

items: MVCC rewrites the entire row and re-TOASTs the whole document
Every index on the table is touched unless the update qualifies as HOT
40 KB document with a hit counter: 40 KB tuple plus WAL per increment
Move the counter to its own column

blocks.title: Concurrency
items: Two read-modify-writes = last-writer-wins loss
Serialize with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
Or mutate in one statement so the row lock covers it
`jsonb_strip_nulls` cleans keys the patch set to null
`jsonb_each` works on objects only
The `_text` variants unquote the scalars for you

lines: -- keep rows with no items instead:

items: Put set-returning functions in `FROM`, not in the SELECT list
`CROSS JOIN LATERAL` drops rows with an empty or missing array
`LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` keeps them

lines: jsonb_to_record(v)   AS x(id int, name text)
jsonb_to_recordset(v) AS x(sku text, qty int)

items: The `AS` column list is mandatory — the type is only known at parse time
`jsonb_to_recordset` handles an array of objects: the bulk-load path
`populate_record` reuses an existing composite or table rowtype instead

slides.page_title: Rows Back to Documents, and jsonpath Basics

items: `jsonb_agg(expr)` collects rows into a JSON array
`jsonb_object_agg(k, v)` collects them into an object
Empty group returns NULL, not `[]` — `coalesce(jsonb_agg(x),'[]'::jsonb)`
Order is explicit: `jsonb_agg(item ORDER BY item->>'sku')`
`FILTER (WHERE item->>'state' = 'ok')` composes with both

blocks.title: Filter First, Unnest Second
blocks.text: Unnesting a million documents to filter them scans everything. Cut the row set with `@>` or jsonpath first, then unnest the survivors — and `jsonb_path_query` often replaces a chain of nested `jsonb_array_elements` calls outright.

items: `jsonpath` is its own type, added in PG 12
Think XPath for JSON
`$` is the root document
`.**` is recursive descent: `$.**.id` finds every `id` at any depth
`$.**{2}` limits how many levels it walks

slides.page_title: jsonpath Filters, Lax vs Strict, Operators

items: `?()` is the filter, `@` is the current item
Predicates: `== != < <= > >=`, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `exists()`, `is unknown`
Methods: `.type() .size() .double() .abs() .floor() .ceiling()`
Also `.keyvalue()` and `.datetime(template)`
Lax unwrapping is why `$.tags ? (@ == "sql")` works for a string or an array
Convenient, and occasionally a lie

caption.text: Most Postgres jsonb bugs are not bugs — they are two operators that look identical and behave nothing alike. `data->>'k' = 'v'` cannot touch a GIN index; `data @> '{"k":"v"}'` can. Ten pages on storage, containment, jsonpath, GIN opclasses, TOAST, and the exact moment a key stops belonging in the document.
